name: Yara Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at the Millbrook River Trust, a small environmental charity with eighteen staff and about three hundred volunteers. I do the diaries, the volunteer rota, the filing, the board papers, and I order everything from waders to printer ink. Last year I built the volunteer rota in a spreadsheet that an AI assistant fills in from people's emails, which saved me about a day a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI tools a lot, then?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. Drafting letters, sorting the shared inbox, turning the director's voice notes into minutes. What wears me out isn't the work, it's being the only person who knows how the systems work, so when I'm on holiday everything breaks and I get texts on the beach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I've got plans for these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic, and I'd keep showing people at the Trust the bits that actually save time. Online I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about how I said the hype was overblown, even though I didn't really say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'm the person who already uses the tools, so I'd be a bit more valuable, not less. The only pressure on me is the usual charity one: our main grant gets renewed every three years and the next one is due in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep automating the boring bits, like the expense forms next. I'd ask for a small pay rise in my review in March, because I've basically taken a day a week of work off the payroll. And I'd keep my savings where they are, about four months, in case the grant falls through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. I like change, and nothing changing is a bit boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the grant fell through in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for another charity job, there are a few in town. Four months of savings and two flatmates splitting the rent means I'd be okay for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay rise. Do you think you'd get it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not the whole thing. Charities pay in thank-you cards, as my director Amara always jokes. But it's worth showing them the number.

I'd post a slightly **smug thread** saying the hype was overblown.
think: Already using the tools makes me **more valuable**, not less.
The real risk is the **2028 grant renewal**, not AI.
do: Automate the **expense forms** next, after the volunteer rota.
Ask for a **pay rise** in the March review.
Keep about **four months** of savings in case the grant falls through.
feel: Calm but **restless**, because she likes change.
S0.quote: Charities pay in thank-you cards, as my director Amara always jokes.
fieldNote: She sees **daily AI use** as a strength in a quiet world.

steps.text: Automate the Trust's expense forms with the AI assistant
Ask for a pay rise at the March review
Keep four months of savings in case the grant ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's more interesting. And also a bit close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when charities have to decide whether they're using AI to do more good or just to cut staff. I'd post about it, and I'd tell the trustees we should use the time saved on more river work, not fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes completely. Half of what I do is on that list: booking, ordering, writing letters. I'd probably keep a job because I'm the one who runs the tools, but it would be a different job, and maybe a lonelier one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Amara to turn my role into something like operations and systems, and I'd do an online course in data and automation over the winter, maybe £400. I'd also join the charity workers' union, which I've meant to do for ages. Savings stay the same; I'm not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit excited, a bit uneasy. Like moving house: you want it, but you don't want to pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lonelier. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I talk to everyone because everyone needs something from me. If the tools do the booking and ordering, people just click a button, and I become the person behind the curtain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the Trust would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin, our finance assistant. He's lovely, but he does exactly the checking and invoicing the card talks about, and he hates computers.

say: Charities must choose: **more good** with AI, or just fewer staff.
Time saved should go on **river work**, not on cutting people.
think: Half my job is on **that list**, so my role changes completely.
I'd likely keep a job, but a **lonelier one** behind the scenes.
do: Ask Amara to turn the role into **operations and systems**.
Take a **£400 online course** in data and automation this winter.
Join the **charity workers' union** I've meant to join for ages.
feel: A bit **excited**, a bit uneasy, like packing to move house.

fieldNote: She expects her job to **change, not vanish**, because she runs the tools.

She worries more for a colleague, **Kevin**, than for herself.

steps.text: Ask the director to rename the job operations and systems
Take a £400 online course in data and automation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's the same year as our grant. Funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income, now, not after the damage. And that the AI companies should pay for it. I'd be loud about it online and I'd go to anything organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think being good with AI tools stops mattering once the AI can set itself up. My edge is being the person in the middle, and full AGI doesn't need a middle person. The three years before robots don't help an admin job, but they do help someone who goes outdoors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd learn everything I can about the field side of the Trust, like river surveys and habitat work, because that's hands-on and gets the extra three years. I'd volunteer on weekend surveys to get the experience. I'd cut my spending on eating out and clothes, and keep the four months of savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit dizzy. I'm usually the one who's fine with change, and this is fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the field work gets three extra years. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I'd be 32 in 2031, and I'd have to hope there's something new by then that needs people. I'm not going to pretend I know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stop paying for the expensive gym and start saving. One of them is a junior lawyer, and I think she's in a worse spot than me.

say: We need a **basic income** now, paid for by the AI companies.
I'd be **loud online** and turn up to anything organised.
think: Being good with AI **stops mattering** once it sets itself up.
The **three-year gap** helps outdoor work, not an admin job.

feel: A bit **dizzy**, because this is fast even for her.

fieldNote: Her usual **confidence cracks**: her AI skill stops being protection.
She uses the **robot delay** deliberately, moving towards outdoor field work.
She's honest that she **doesn't know** what comes after 2031.

steps.text: Learn river surveys and habitat work from the field team
Volunteer on weekend river surveys for experience
Cut eating out and new clothes
Campaign online for a basic income paid by AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a deadline, not a delay, and charities should start planning now. I'd probably give a talk at the regional charity meetup about how we used the tools and what we'd do differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for the first three or four years, because I'd be the person helping small charities switch over. After that, same problem as the fast one. Being early helps until everyone has caught up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start doing paid weekend work setting up AI systems for other small charities, maybe £200 a day. I'd put that money straight into savings to get to six months or more. And I'd start a part-time ecology certificate, so I've got the field route ready for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with an alarm clock ticking somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a lot at once, a side business and a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd probably drop one by the summer. If I had to choose, I'd keep the course, because the side business has a shelf life and the field skills don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the Trust's office in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it shrinks to me and the tools by about 2030. Amara would try to keep people, but the funders would ask why a charity is paying for work a machine can do.

say: Five years is a **deadline, not a delay**, for charities to plan.
I'd give a talk at the **regional charity meetup** on what we learned.
think: I'd **do well** for three or four years helping small charities switch.

fieldNote: She sees a **window** of a few years where her skills pay well.
She builds a **second route** on purpose, through field ecology.

steps.text: Set up AI systems for other small charities at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, and I'd push for a basic income trial now, while there's time to test it. I'd talk it up with anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel good about my chances. I've got time to build a career in operations, then move into field work or something new before 2036. The risk is that ten years feels long and charities are slow, so I'd have to be the one pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd take the operations course and ask for the systems role at the Trust. I'd keep doing a bit of freelance setup for other charities. And I'd finally move in with my boyfriend Tariq, since we'd been waiting until things felt settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Uneasy at the edges, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the move with Tariq depend on this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd both want to know we can each pay half for a while. Tariq teaches primary school, which feels safer in all of these than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in the charity world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. I'd rather help a river than help a bank save money. That doesn't change whether it's two years or ten.

I'd **talk it up** with anyone who'd listen.

Charities are **slow**, so I'd have to keep pushing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one worries me most. Being early is my usual trick, and AGI by 2028 is the only picture where being early doesn't work. What would help is a basic income or something like it, and free training in hands-on fields like ecology, so people can move before the robots come.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would miss. For me it's the office chat, the person who comes in soaking wet from the river and wants a cup of tea. A machine running the diary won't make that tea.

headlineQuote: Being early is my usual trick, and AGI by 2028 is the only picture where being early doesn't work.
portrait: Yara, 27, is the office administrator at the **Millbrook River Trust**, a small environmental charity.
She uses **AI tools every day** and built the volunteer rota around one.
In slower pictures she expects her job to **change, not vanish**, and plans a systems role.
In the fast AGI picture her **edge disappears**, and she turns towards hands-on field ecology.
She wants a **basic income** and keeps choosing charity work over higher pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the only picture where being an early AI user doesn't protect her.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or something like it.
**Free training** in hands-on fields like ecology.
